scope_notes: Covers posture/trunk lean, foot placement and overstriding, cadence/step length, arm swing, and pelvis/knee control (pelvic drop, crossover). Aimed at recreational to competitive runners on flat ground. Hills, racing tactics and footwear are not covered.
source_gap_notes: Strong research base (ACSM clinical guidance, cadence-retraining trials, running-economy reviews). The research explicitly warns there is no single 'correct' technique, so most rules are framed as injury-risk or economy flags rather than absolutes.

sources.name: ACSM - Healthy Habits for Distance Running (Vincent & Vincent, 2022)
sources.credibility: American College of Sports Medicine infographic + evidence summary: cadence, short quick steps, step width, glutes/kneecaps forward, soft landings, chin tuck/slight lean, linear arm swing, fatigue breaks.

sources.name: Healthy Running Habits for the Distance Runner: Clinical Utility of the ACSM Infographic (Current Sports Medicine Reports 2022)
Heiderscheit BC et al. - Effects of step rate manipulation on joint mechanics during running (Med Sci Sports Exerc 2011)
sources.credibility: +5-10% step rate at the same speed reduced vertical COM excursion and hip/knee loading (knee energy absorption reduced ~20% at +5% and ~34% at +10%).

sources.name: Schubert AG, Kempf J, Heiderscheit BC - Influence of Stride Frequency and Length on Running Mechanics: systematic review (Sports Health 2014)
sources.credibility: Higher stride rate consistently reduces joint loading, GRF and shock.

sources.name: Chan ZYS et al. - Gait Retraining for the Reduction of Injury Occurrence in Novice Distance Runners: 1-year RCT (AJSM 2018)
sources.credibility: Two weeks of gait retraining (soft landing) -> ~62% lower injury risk over 12 months.

sources.name: Effects of 12-week cadence retraining on impact peak, load rates and lower extremity biomechanics (PMC)
sources.credibility: Graduated cadence retraining reduced impact peak and loading rates; cadence increase persisted.

sources.name: Folland JP et al. - Running Technique is an Important Component of Running Economy and Performance (MSSE 2017)
sources.credibility: Technique explained ~39% of energy-cost variance: less vertical pelvis oscillation, less braking, less knee flexion in stance; shank angle at touchdown, duty factor and trunk lean related to performance.

sources.name: Moore IS - Is There an Economical Running Technique? Review of Modifiable Biomechanical Factors (Sports Medicine 2016)
sources.credibility: Supports lower vertical oscillation, efficient propulsion; cautions against a universal technique.

sources.name: Special Olympics Athletics Coaches Quick Start Guide - Running Mechanics
sources.credibility: Simple coaching-level cues for posture, arm and leg action.

sources.name: Athletics South Africa - Level 1 Coaching Manual: Distance Races
sources.credibility: National federation coach-education manual for middle/long distance.
sources.usage_note: Background: national federation coach-education manual; not cited for a specific item.

skills.name: Posture and trunk lean
skills.recommended_camera: Side view at hip height, treadmill or track, 60+ fps; film after 10+ min of running and again when fatigued.

checkpoints.description: Tall posture with a slight whole-body forward lean from the ankles - not bending at the waist, not leading with the head.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: trunk (hip->shoulder) lean ~5-10 deg forward of vertical; hip angle not flexed (no 'sitting'); ear roughly over the shoulder

checkpoints.description: Head neutral, chin slightly tucked, eyes ahead.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: ear-to-shoulder line near vertical; head not jutting forward

faults.name: Bent at the waist / excessive forward lean
faults.video_signs: Trunk folded forward at the hips; often worsens with fatigue.
faults.correction_cue: 'Run tall - pull a string up through your spine; tuck the chin.'
faults.why_it_matters: Moderate-to-high trunk flexion increases foot reach ahead of the body and loading rate, and can strain the low back and hamstrings.

faults.name: Leaning back / sitting
faults.video_signs: Trunk behind vertical, hips low and behind the feet.
faults.correction_cue: 'Slight lean from the ankles - hips forward.'
faults.why_it_matters: Backward lean promotes overstriding and braking.

drills.name: Fatigue form check and walk breaks
drills.setup: Plan intervals or route loops where form can be checked.
steps: Note signs of form breakdown: louder footfalls, longer steps, arms crossing, more lean.
Take a walk break or shorten the interval when these appear.
drills.fixes: Bent at the waist; overstriding when tired
drills.why: Fatigue increases trunk lean, hip adduction and contact time; breaking up runs limits exposure to degraded mechanics.

pro_tips.tip: Cues like 'lean from the ankles' are often misread as bending at the waist; ACSM authors find 'tuck in the chin' or 'pull a string up through the head' work better for many runners.

skills.name: Foot placement and overstriding
skills.recommended_camera: Side view at ground level, 120+ fps (treadmill ideal).

checkpoints.description: Foot lands close to beneath the centre of mass (short 'reach'), with the knee slightly flexed - not far out in front with a straight knee.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: horizontal heel/ankle-to-hip distance at initial contact small (e.g., < ~15-20% of leg length); knee flexed at contact (< ~170 deg)

checkpoints.description: Shank (shin) near vertical at touchdown rather than angled forward ahead of the knee.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: shank angle at touchdown within ~0-10 deg of vertical

checkpoints.description: Soft, quiet landings (any strike pattern) rather than a hard heel slam.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: no single rule - audio loudness and knee/ankle flexion during loading are proxies

faults.name: Overstriding (reaching heel strike)
faults.video_signs: Heel lands well ahead of the body with a nearly straight knee and dorsiflexed foot; braking 'jolt' visible.
faults.correction_cue: 'Short, quick steps - land under your hips.'
faults.why_it_matters: Long reaching steps increase braking, tibial shock and knee loading.

faults.name: Loud, heavy footfalls
faults.video_signs: Audible slapping; visible jarring on contact.
faults.why_it_matters: Soft-landing retraining reduced impact loading and injury incidence in novice runners.

drills.name: Soft-landing retraining sessions
drills.setup: Treadmill or quiet track; optional real-time feedback (mirror, video, sound).
steps: Run at easy pace and cue 'land softly and quietly'.
Let the runner explore strategies (strike pattern, knee bend) to reduce noise.
drills.dosage: Short retraining blocks (e.g., several sessions over ~2 weeks), integrated into easy runs
drills.why: Feedback-based soft-landing retraining reduced loading rates and was associated with ~62% lower injury risk over a year in novices.

pro_tips.tip: Low evidence links any particular foot-strike type to injury; focus on soft, quiet landings rather than forcing a forefoot strike.

skills.name: Cadence and step length
skills.recommended_camera: Side view; count steps over 30-60 s or use a watch/app.

checkpoints.description: Cadence appropriate to speed; many runners benefit from +5-10% above their habitual cadence, often landing above ~170 steps/min.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: steps/min = foot contacts per minute; flag if < ~160-165 spm at easy pace AND overstriding is present

checkpoints.description: Low vertical bounce of the pelvis.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: vertical hip oscillation ~5-10 cm (lower generally more economical)

faults.name: Low cadence with long bouncy strides
faults.video_signs: Few steps per minute, big vertical oscillation, foot reaching ahead.
faults.why_it_matters: Raising cadence reduces vertical excursion, braking and knee energy absorption.

drills.name: Metronome cadence retraining
drills.setup: Metronome app or watch beep set to habitual cadence +5-7.5%.
steps: Measure habitual cadence at easy pace.
Run segments matching the metronome at the same speed.
Gradually increase segment duration over weeks, then wean off the metronome.
drills.dosage: Start 3-5 x 2-3 min within easy runs; build over ~4-12 weeks
drills.why: Auditory pacing is the method used in lab and field studies to raise cadence, which reduced impact and loading rates, with changes that persisted.

pro_tips.tip: Heiderscheit et al. found +5% step rate reduced knee energy absorption ~20% and +10% ~34% at the same speed.
Cadence and short-quick-step cues are the first, highest-impact changes recommended in the ACSM healthy-running-habits guidance.

checkpoints.description: Arms swing forward and back from relaxed shoulders, elbows roughly 90 degrees, hands not crossing the midline.
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: elbow angle ~70-110 deg; wrists stay on their own side of the body midline (front view)

faults.name: Arms crossing the body / excessive rotation
faults.video_signs: Hands swing across the chest; shoulders twist.
faults.correction_cue: 'Swing like a pendulum - hands brush the hips, forward and back.'
faults.why_it_matters: Linear arm swing helps counter lower-body rotation; crossing increases torso rotation and can indicate fatigue.

faults.name: Shrugged, tense shoulders
faults.video_signs: Shoulders near the ears; fists clenched.

drills.name: Standing / walking arm-swing drill
drills.setup: Stand or walk in front of a mirror.
steps: Swing arms forward and back from relaxed shoulders, elbows ~90 deg.
Hands travel from about chest height to the hip, without crossing the midline.
drills.dosage: 3 x 30 s standing, then 4 x 80 m strides
drills.why: Isolating the arm pattern without running fatigue makes the linear swing easier to feel.

pro_tips.tip: Arms crossing the body is one of ACSM's signs of fatigue-degraded form - a cue to take a break.

skills.name: Pelvis and knee control (pelvic drop, crossover)
skills.recommended_camera: Rear view (behind treadmill) at hip height, 60+ fps.

checkpoints.description: Pelvis stays nearly level in single-leg stance (limited contralateral pelvic drop).
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: no fixed cutoff: measure contralateral pelvic drop (hip-line tilt) at mid-stance and track it over time - runners in the ACSM authors' clinic averaged ~11 deg before and ~9.5 deg after retraining

checkpoints.description: Kneecaps point forward; knee doesn't collapse inward (hip adduction/internal rotation).
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: frontal-plane knee projection angle small (< ~10 deg valgus)

checkpoints.description: Adequate step width - feet don't cross the midline ('running on a tightrope').
checkpoints.measurable_angle_or_rule: each foot lands on its own side of the body midline

faults.name: Contralateral pelvic drop / hip adduction
faults.video_signs: Opposite hip drops in stance; knee drifts inward.
faults.correction_cue: 'Squeeze your glutes, kneecaps forward, keep your hips level.'
faults.why_it_matters: Associated with patellofemoral pain, IT-band and tibial stress issues; cueing with mirror feedback reduced it in trials.

faults.name: Crossover gait
faults.video_signs: Feet land on or across the midline.
faults.correction_cue: 'Run with one foot on each side of a road line.'
faults.why_it_matters: Narrow steps increase tibial stress; widening step width reduces hip adduction and knee loading.

drills.name: Mirror hip-control retraining
drills.setup: Treadmill facing a mirror (or real-time video).
steps: Run at easy pace and cue: 'squeeze your glutes, kneecaps pointing forward, hips level'.
Use the mirror to watch knee and pelvis alignment.
Gradually reduce mirror feedback over sessions.
drills.dosage: 10-15 min within easy runs, several sessions over 2-8 weeks
drills.why: Mirror and verbal-cue retraining reduced hip adduction and pelvic drop and eased knee pain in trials reported by ACSM.

drills.name: Road-line step-width drill
drills.setup: A painted line (track lane line or road line).
steps: Run with the left foot on the left of the line and the right foot on the right.
Alternative cues: 'pedal a bike wide enough' or 'jump rope moving forward'.
drills.why: Visual cueing widens step width, which reduces hip adduction and tibial stress.

pro_tips.tip: Introduce one or two big cues first (cadence, soft landings); smaller cues (glutes, arms, lean) often fix themselves afterward.
There is no universal economical running technique - individualize and change form gradually while strengthening the kinetic chain.
